message.content:
Below is a **complete, ready‑to‑run example** that shows how to create a Google Cloud Compute Engine instance that has a GPU attached and runs Ubuntu 20.04 LTS.  
Because Google Cloud does **not** offer an “RTX A6000” GPU (the closest is the NVIDIA Tesla A100), the example uses the **Tesla A100** accelerator. If you really need an RTX A6000 you would have to wait until Google Cloud adds that GPU type or use a different provider.

---

## 1. Prerequisites

| Step | What you need | How to get it |
|------|---------------|---------------|
| 1 | **Google Cloud project** | Create one in the [Cloud Console](https://console.cloud.google.com/) |
| 2 | **Billing enabled** | Enable billing for the project |
| 3 | **Compute Engine API enabled** | In the Cloud Console → APIs & Services → Library → Search for “Compute Engine API” → Enable |
| 4 | **OAuth 2.0 access token** | You can obtain one via `gcloud auth application-default print-access-token` or by using a service account key |
| 5 | **Zone with GPU availability** | Not all zones support GPUs. Check the [GPU availability table](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/gpus#available_zones) and pick one (e.g., `us-central1-a`) |

---

## 2. Using the `gcloud` CLI

```bash
# 1️⃣ Authenticate (if you haven’t already)
gcloud auth login

# 2️⃣ Set your project
gcloud config set project YOUR_PROJECT_ID

# 3️⃣ Create the instance
gcloud compute instances create my-gpu-instance \
    --zone us-central1-a \
    --machine-type n1-standard-8 \          # 8 vCPUs, 30 GB RAM
    --accelerator type=nvidia-tesla-a100,count=1 \   # 1 A100 GPU
    --image-project ubuntu-os-cloud \
    --image-family ubuntu-2004-lts \
    --boot-disk-size 50GB \
    --boot-disk-type pd-ssd \
    --maintenance-policy TERMINATE \
    --restart-on-failure
```

### What each flag does

| Flag | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `--zone` | The Compute Engine zone where the instance will live |
| `--machine-type` | CPU/RAM configuration |
| `--accelerator` | Attach a GPU (`type` + `count`) |
| `--image-project` / `--image-family` | Base OS image (Ubuntu 20.04 LTS) |
| `--boot-disk-size` / `--boot-disk-type` | Size & type of the boot disk |
| `--maintenance-policy` | How to handle maintenance events (`TERMINATE` means the VM will be stopped and restarted) |
| `--restart-on-failure` | Auto‑restart if the VM crashes |

> **Tip:** If you want to use a **different GPU** (e.g., `nvidia-tesla-p100`), just change the `type` value.

---

## 3. Using the REST API (JSON)

If you prefer to call the Compute Engine REST API directly (e.g., from a script or a custom tool), here’s the exact HTTP request you would send:

```http
POST https://compute.googleapis.com/compute/v1/projects/YOUR_PROJECT_ID/zones/us-central1-a/instances
Authorization: Bearer ACCESS_TOKEN
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "name": "my-gpu-instance",
  "machineType": "zones/us-central1-a/machineTypes/n1-standard-8",
  "disks": [
    {
      "boot": true,
      "autoDelete": true,
      "initializeParams": {
        "sourceImage": "projects/ubuntu-os-cloud/global/images/family/ubuntu-2004-lts",
        "diskSizeGb": 50,
        "diskType": "zones/us-central1-a/diskTypes/pd-ssd"
      }
    }
  ],
  "guestAccelerators": [
    {
      "acceleratorCount": 1,
      "acceleratorType": "projects/YOUR_PROJECT_ID/zones/us-central1-a/acceleratorTypes/nvidia-tesla-a100"
    }
  ],
  "scheduling": {
    "automaticRestart": true,
    "onHostMaintenance": "TERMINATE"
  },
  "metadata": {
    "items": [
      {
        "key": "startup-script",
        "value": "#!/bin/bash\napt-get update\napt-get install -y cuda-toolkit-11-4"
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

### How to send it

```bash
curl -X POST \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth application-default print-access-token)" \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     -d @instance.json \
     "https://compute.googleapis.com/compute/v1/projects/YOUR_PROJECT_ID/zones/us-central1-a/instances"
```

> Replace `YOUR_PROJECT_ID` with your actual project ID and `ACCESS_TOKEN` with a valid OAuth 2.0 token.  
> Save the JSON body above into a file called `instance.json` and run the `curl` command.

---

## 4. Quick sanity check

After the instance is created, you can verify that the GPU is attached:

```bash
gcloud compute instances describe my-gpu-instance --zone us-central1-a | grep -i gpu
```

You should see something like:

```
guestAccelerators:
- acceleratorCount: 1
  acceleratorType: projects/YOUR_PROJECT_ID/zones/us-central1-a/acceleratorTypes/nvidia-tesla-a100
```

---

## 5. Common pitfalls & troubleshooting

| Issue | Fix |
|-------|-----|
| **“No GPUs available in this zone”** | Pick a zone that supports GPUs (see the availability table). |
| **“Quota exceeded”** | Request a GPU quota increase in the Cloud Console → IAM & Admin → Quotas. |
| **“Access denied”** | Ensure your OAuth token has the `https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform` scope. |
| **“Image not found”** | Double‑check the image family (`ubuntu-2004-lts`) and project (`ubuntu-os-cloud`). |

---

## 6. Wrap‑up

* **Command‑line**: `gcloud compute instances create …` – quick, interactive, great for ad‑hoc tasks.  
* **REST API**: POST to `/instances` – ideal for automation, CI/CD pipelines, or custom tooling.  

Both approaches give you the same result: a Compute Engine VM running Ubuntu 20.04 LTS with a Tesla A100 GPU attached. Adjust the `machineType`, `acceleratorType`, and `imageFamily` values to fit your exact requirements. Happy computing!
